snippet.title: The Truth About Bidirectional EV Chargers (Right Now)❗❗❗ #evcharging #wallbox #goe
snippet.description:
Bidirectional charging is currently only possible with DC systems – and affordable DC chargers are rare. And guess what? As of now, no electric car fully supports AC bidirectional charging. The only version that actually works today is Vehicle-to-Load. 

Vehicle-to-Home and Vehicle-to-Grid? Not yet.

So, if you’re buying a “bidirectional” charger, it just means the hardware’s ready, but the software and regulations aren’t. You will still not be able to power your home or the grid with your AC charger yet - not without limitations.

snippet.title: Vehicle-To-Grid (V2G): The Key to the Energy Transition?
snippet.description:
Vehicle-to-Grid - the key to energy transition? Yes, most probably, but there are still quite a few hurdles to overcome - legal ones, technical ones, and even a few psychological ones. 

▬ Video Content ▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬

▬ Battery wear because of V2G? ▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬ 
Many people worry that frequent charging and discharging might wear out their car’s battery faster, shortening its lifespan and eventually leading to higher replacement costs. In reality, the typical discharge rate for bidirectional charging is around three kilowatts. This is so low that it’s very unlikely to harm your battery at all. In fact, when charging bidirectionally at home using an AC charger, the power levels are gentle enough that it’s generally considered safe.
And to be extra cautious, some car manufacturers are already building in protective limits. Volkswagen, for instance, sets a minimum battery level of 20 percent during bidirectional DC charging - just to reduce any potential stress on the battery.

▬ Financial benefits are unclear ▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬ 
Right now, no one can promise that the actual payments would be enough to make it worthwhile.
Take this example: You charge your car at home for 15 cents per kilowatt-hour, then park it overnight. If you were to sell that electricity back to the grid, the operator might only pay you 5 cents per kilowatt-hour. Why? Because there’s currently no system in place to properly negotiate or set the price.

▬ Clearer Communication needed ▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬ 
People need to understand the real benefits - for example, that V2G could lower their energy costs if the system’s designed the right way. Manufacturers should also be more transparent about battery health and how warranties might change once bidirectional charging becomes mainstream. 

▬ Technical Hurdles ▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬ 
One major step is finalising ISO 15118-20 for AC charging. That’s the international standard that allows cars and chargers to “talk” to each other - it’s the foundation for Vehicle-to-Grid. It’s already been completed for DC charging, but the AC version is still in progress. 

▬ Legal & Economic Hurdles ▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬▬ 
And then there’s the legal and economic side. Countries like France are already quite advanced in setting up clear rules and incentives. Other countries, like Germany, are still ironing out things like taxation, regulations, and financial rewards for participants. Why the difference? It often comes down to politics, the national energy mix, and how much flexibility a country’s grid needs.

In Germany, for instance, with its strong focus on renewables like solar and wind, Vehicle-to-Grid could help stabilize the grid massively, by storing excess green energy during peak production, and balancing the grid during peak demand. But Germany still lags behind - partly due to political and regulatory delays.

In contrast, Austria, with its heavy reliance on hydropower, has less need for such systems because hydropower is already quite stable. Countries like Poland or France, which have a more traditional energy mix, only offer moderate incentives for peak load management.

France is leading the way in bidirectional charging - thanks to strong political support for the energy transition and sustainability goals. And with a rapidly growing EV market, France has the perfect testing ground for rolling out this technology at scale.

Now, of course, Vehicle-to-Grid could technically reach market maturity before all these questions are fully answered  but can we really call it “mature” if the system surrounding it isn’t ready yet?
Finally, let’s not forget the hardware. To make Vehicle-to-Grid work, wallboxes and charging stations need to support bidirectional power flow - both in hardware and software.

Some DC chargers can already do that - but they’re very expensive. That’s why manufacturers like go-e are working on affordable wallboxes that are already equipped with the right hardware.
The only thing missing? The software - especially for real-time energy exchange and billing. And that can’t be fully developed until the legal and market frameworks are in place.

In practice, the tech isn’t quite usable yet - because ISO 15118-20 for AC charging is unfinished, real-time billing software is still missing, and the legal groundwork is still being laid.

Did I make a massive, $15,000 mistake trying to heat my well-insulated shed with only off-grid solar power? We built a 12x16 shed office and installed an insanely capable 6kW solar system, but when winter hit, we quickly learned the truth about trying to heat a shed completely off-grid.

In this video, we put a 1500W electric radiator to the 24-hour test to answer two essential questions:

1)  Can a standard 1500W electric heater heat a 12x16 insulated space? (Yes, it can!)

2)  Is off-grid solar for heating a viable solution? (The answer might surprise you!)

We break down the real cost of heating the shed using grid-tied power ($3.17 per day) vs. the massive, energy-sapping demands of an off-grid system, showing why an expensive 6kW solar system still falls short during overcast, winter weather.

snippet.title: How to Build a Floating Deck — No Permits, No Experience Needed
snippet.description:
Adjustable Pedestal (10-Pack):  https://geni.us/dji6
Camo Screws (1 7/8"):  https://geni.us/Sg84i
Camo Jig:  https://geni.us/B0G1Ziw
Camo Board Bending Tool:  https://geni.us/etZl

In this video, I'll show you step by step how to build a DIY floating deck using adjustable pedestals — no permits, no handrails, and no perfectly level ground required. If you've been using TuffBlocks or concrete blocks, this method will save you hours of site prep.  Unlike TuffBlocks or CAMO blocks that require your entire ground surface to be perfectly level, adjustable pedestals give you an inch of adjustment built in — plus 1", 2", and 4" extensions for sloped ground. I built this 6'x16' floating deck alongside my 12x16 modern shed office conversion, and the pedestals made leveling a breeze.

CHAPTERS
0:00 — Why a floating deck?
0:28 — Measuring & planning your layout
1:05 — Adjustable pedestals vs TuffBlocks
1:44 — Setting your 4x4 posts
2:39 — Why I don't use TuffBlocks or CAMO blocks
3:39 — Framing the floor joists (16" on center)
6:21 — Installing deck boards (zero cuts!)
7:09 — Using the CAMO hidden fastener system
9:23 — The finished floating deck

MATERIALS USED
2x 16' pressure-treated 4x4 posts
Pressure-treated 2x4 joists (16" on center)
5/4 pressure-treated deck boards (16')
Adjustable pedestals with extensions
CAMO hidden fastener system
GRK 4" #10 screws (end grain)
SPAX 3.25" screws (toenailing)

TOOLS
4' bubble level
Klein Tools Laser level
Speed square
Camo Board bender (don't skip this one!)
Camo jig
